findings.label: Mite-bite eschar
findings.evidence: Eschar on posterior right calf of patient with rickettsialpox.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph explicitly captioned as an eschar on the posterior right calf of a patient with rickettsialpox; the eschar is the classic inoculation lesion (mite-bite eschar) of rickettsialpox. A magenta highlight ring is present on the image.
panels.attribution_text: Krusell et al. Rickettsialpox in North Carolina: a case report.. Emerging infectious diseases 2002. doi:10.3201/eid0807.010501. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Eschar on posterior right calf of patient with rickettsialpox.
in_text_mentions: On admission, the patient appeared ill and was febrile. An eschar was present on his posterior right lower leg (Figure 1). Approximately 30 erythematous macules were noted on his trunk, arms, and legs (Figures 2 and 3). Many of these macules had small central vesicles. Laboratory testing showed normal values for electrolytes and creatinine, hematocrit, and leukocytes. His platelet count was 85,000/mm3. Routine blood cultures were sterile.

Rickettsialpox may have occurred sporadically in North Carolina in the past, but the incidence of this disease in this state is probably extremely low. As Figures 1–3 illustrate, infection with R. akari produces unusual and characteristic skin abnormalities. Because cases of rickettsialpox may be confused with chickenpox or other viral exanthematous diseases, misdiagnosis may occur when sporadic cases occur in areas where the disease is unknown to local practitioners.
